tool_args.old_string: We evaluate on ALFWorld~\citep{shridhar2021alfworld}, a text-based household environment with six task types requiring sequential reasoning over up to 50 steps. The environment provides ternary reward: $R \in \{r_-, 0, r_+\}$, where $r_- = -0.1$ per invalid action, $0$ for valid but unsuccessful actions, and $r_+$ for task success. Our theoretical analysis (Section~\ref{sec:theory}) assumes the simplified binary case ($R \in \{0, r_+\}$), which yields an upper bound on sign misattribution severity; Section~\ref{sec:sign_verification} validates this bound under both reward structures. The base policy is Qwen3-1.7B fine-tuned on expert demonstrations (SFT baseline: 12.5\% in-distribution). At this baseline success rate, Proposition~2 predicts the majority of gradient updates carry incorrect sign. All conditions use RAGEN~\citep{ragen2025} (v0.1, commit \texttt{3a6b48b})\footnote{Our implementation extends RAGEN v0.1 with episode-level training support. Code available upon acceptance.} with GRPO~\citep{shao2024deepseekmath} ($K{=}8$; full hyperparameters in Appendix~\ref{app:hyperparameters}). We report success rate on a 134-task OOD set (primary) and 32-task in-distribution set (secondary). Seed counts are noted per condition.

tool_args.old_string: Step-independent training fails through two mechanisms: information loss imposes a constant performance ceiling while sign misattribution causes cumulative degradation. A partial factorial experiment isolates each mechanism's contribution, and direct sign measurement confirms the theoretical prediction that credit agreement drops to near-random levels. Episode-level GRPO structurally eliminates both failure modes, though the fix is seed-dependent: only 36\% of seeds achieve significant OOD generalization, pointing to initialization sensitivity as an open problem. The dual-mechanism framework provides a post-hoc explanation for why concurrent methods with finer-grained credit~\citep{hcapo2026,feng2025gigpo,turnppo2025} succeed by eliminating sign misattribution. This finding applies to GRPO-style methods under step-level windowing, sparse reward, and group-relative normalization, verified on GRPO in ALFWorld and ScienceWorld.
tool_args.new_string: Step-independent training fails through two co-symbiotic mechanisms: information loss imposes a constant ceiling while sign misattribution causes cumulative degradation. Episode-level GRPO structurally eliminates both, though the fix is seed-dependent (36\% generalize significantly). This finding applies to GRPO-style methods under step-level windowing, sparse reward, and group-relative normalization, verified on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld.

This non-additive interaction means the mechanisms cannot be cleanly separated; the partial factorial isolates their \textit{marginal} contributions but not their joint behavior (Appendix~\ref{app:why_defaults}).

14	We implement the partial factorial design from Section~\ref{sec:factorial_design} (3 of 4 cells; Cell~C excluded due to NaN instability) with two seeds per condition. Cell~C (full observation, step-level advantage) would isolate M2 without M1, but we encountered persistent training instability in this configuration (Appendix~\ref{app:cell_c}). Cell~C's NaN divergence, qualitatively different from Cell~A's gradual collapse, suggests that information loss may have an unintended stabilizing effect on gradient variance, questioning the approximate separability assumed by the partial factorial (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
15

241	\label{app:early_signal}
242	
243	We investigated whether early training signals (steps 1--3) can predict seed-level generalization outcomes. We analyze 12 seeds grouped into three outcome categories following the definitions in Section~\ref{sec:seed_variability}: Generalized ($n{=}4$), Stagnant ($n{=}4$), and Collapsed ($n{=}4$, including seed7, which received a subsequent KL penalty intervention and is excluded from Table~\ref{tab:seed_variability}; its pre-intervention training trajectory is used here). No standard training metric (reward, KL divergence, entropy, gradient norm, response length, or train success rate) showed statistically significant between-group differences in the first three training steps (all Welch $t$-test $p > 0.2$, $n = 4$ per group). Two of the four Collapsed seeds (seed7, seed8) exhibited among the \textit{highest} early rewards and train success rates, with their collapse manifesting only after step~5 through response length inflation or reward degradation.
244	
245	The strongest candidate predictor was the mutual information diversity estimate at step~1, which showed a large effect size (Cohen's $d = 1.11$) favoring Generalized over Collapsed seeds and a trending correlation with final OOD performance (Spearman $\rho = 0.43$, $p = 0.19$), but remained non-significant with the available sample size ($n = 4$ per group). These results suggest that seed-dependent outcomes are governed by mechanisms not captured by standard early training diagnostics, and that early stopping or seed selection based on initial step metrics would be unreliable.
